Field surveys of Pale spotfin croaker (Johnius glaucus) along the northeastern coast of Taiwan have provided detailed life-history metrics for this sciaenid species. Analysis of a large sample of adult specimens revealed that the maximum recorded total length approaches 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], representing the ultimate size attained by the oldest individuals in the population. Corresponding to this length, the ultimate wet weight derived from length-weight relationships is approximately 309 grams [Wwi = approximately 309 grams], a value that positions Johnius glaucus among the medium-sized members of its genus. Notably, the transition to reproductive maturity occurs well before these maximal dimensions are reached. Individuals achieve puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, at a total length of 18.9 centimeters [Lp = 18.9 centimeters]. The body mass associated with this developmental milestone, calculated from the species-specific length-weight equation, is roughly 76 grams [Wwp = roughly 76 grams], indicating that nearly three-quarters of somatic growth potential remains to be realized after the onset of reproductive capability.

Reproductive investment in Johnius glaucus is substantial. Gravid females collected during the primary spawning season in March and April were found to carry large clutches of small, pelagic eggs. The mean fecundity per spawning event was estimated at approximately 181 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 181 eggs per clutch], with individual females capable of producing roughly one clutch per day [F_R_i = roughly one clutch per day] during the peak of the spawning period. This exceptionally high daily spawning frequency yields a considerable daily reproductive output. At the prevailing water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], which represents the thermal conditions of the coastal spawning grounds during the breeding season, the daily reproduction rate is substantial. The combination of moderate clutch size and very high spawning frequency reflects a life-history strategy favoring high fecundity and rapid population turnover, a pattern common among tropical and subtropical sciaenids occupying productive inshore environments.

The early life stages of Johnius glaucus begin with small, transparent, pelagic eggs measuring approximately 1 millimeter in diameter. Upon fertilization, these yolk-laden eggs undergo rapid development, and the newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge at a remarkably small size. The wet weight at birth, determined from the egg diameter using the formula for a sphere with the density of seawater, is approximately 0.00053 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00053 grams]. This minute neonatal mass reflects the energetic strategy of producing vast numbers of small offspring, each with limited endogenous yolk reserves. The lecithotrophic larvae must rapidly develop feeding structures and locate suitable planktonic prey to avoid starvation in the oligotrophic waters they inhabit. Such a minimal investment per individual offspring, combined with the high reproductive output described earlier, characterizes a typical r-selected reproductive strategy, albeit one that requires exceptionally productive nursery habitats in the nearby estuarine zones to ensure adequate larval survival.

Longevity estimates for Johnius glaucus are derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination. Under natural conditions in the warm coastal waters of its range, the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days], which equates to roughly five years when calculations account for the typical thermal regime of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is consistent with a fast-paced life history, where individuals mature early, reproduce intensely during a limited window, and experience high natural mortality rates associated with predation pressure in the shallow, predator-rich habitats they occupy. The age structure of sampled populations typically shows a predominance of young individuals between one and three years of age, with comparatively few fish surviving beyond the fourth year. This pattern of early senescence and short generation time aligns well with the species' observed reproductive characteristics and small terminal body size.

Comparative analyses within the Sciaenidae family reveal that the life-history strategy of Johnius glaucus occupies a distinct position along the continuum from slow to fast life-history paces. The maximum lifespan of 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days] observed in Johnius glaucus is considerably shorter than that reported for larger, more northerly distributed sciaenids such as the Atlantic croaker or the freshwater drum, which may persist for over a decade at a temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. Conversely, the ultimate total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] and the corresponding wet weight at puberty of 76 grams [Wwp = 76 grams] are intermediate when compared to other members of the genus Johnius. This combination of moderate adult size, early maturation, high fecundity, and short lifespan suggests an adaptive response to the relatively stable but predation-intensive environments of tropical coastal ecosystems, where the probability of surviving to advanced ages is low and selective pressure favors early and prolific reproduction.
